q: Basic, predefined and custom roles in GCP IAM: which should you use and why avoid basic roles?
p: Basic roles (Owner, Editor, Viewer) are very broad and span almost every service. Predefined roles are curated per service and job. Custom roles let you pick exact permissions but need maintenance. Prefer predefined, and custom only when none fit.
tip: Say Editor can modify almost everything, including creating service accounts, so it is a privilege escalation path.
a: IAM roles are collections of permissions. Basic roles, Owner, Editor and Viewer, predate the current model and grant hundreds of permissions across nearly all services, so they violate least privilege. Editor, for example, can create resources and service accounts in the project. Predefined roles are maintained by Google for a specific product and task, such as Storage Object Viewer or Cloud SQL Client, and update automatically when new permissions are needed. Custom roles let me assemble an exact permission set, which is useful for tight boundaries, but I must maintain them as APIs change and they have limits on the number of permissions and scope. My approach is to grant predefined roles to groups, never to individual users, at the lowest practical level in the hierarchy, use IAM Recommender to remove unused permissions, add conditions for time or resource constraints, and keep basic roles out of production projects.
f: What does IAM Recommender do?
How do you review role bindings at scale?

q: What are IAM Conditions and IAM deny policies, and how do they differ from allow policies?
p: Allow policies grant access. IAM Conditions add attributes such as time, resource name or tag to a binding. Deny policies explicitly block permissions for principals, evaluated before allow, and apply at the organization, folder or project level.
tip: Deny always wins over allow, so deny policies are a strong guardrail against mistakes in lower-level grants.
a: A normal allow policy binds principals to roles on a resource. An IAM Condition is an attribute-based restriction attached to a binding, so a role applies only when the expression is true, for example only until a date, only on resources with a given name prefix or tag, or only during working hours. That makes temporary or scoped access safer without creating many custom roles. Deny policies are separate: they list principals and permissions that are blocked, optionally with exceptions, and are evaluated before allow policies. Even if someone has a broad role granted lower in the hierarchy, a deny at the organization or folder wins. I use deny policies for guardrails such as preventing everyone except a break-glass group from creating service account keys or disabling audit logs, and I use conditions for just-in-time access combined with approval workflows and logging.
f: In what order are policies evaluated?
How would you grant two hours of temporary admin access?

q: What are the risks of the default service accounts in GCP, and how do you remove them from your design?
p: The Compute Engine default service account is created with the Editor role in older projects and is attached to VMs by default. Any process on the VM inherits it. Use dedicated, least-privilege service accounts per workload and enforce with org policy.
tip: Name the org policy iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts, which stops new projects from granting Editor to default accounts.
a: When the Compute Engine or App Engine API is enabled, Google creates default service accounts, and in many existing projects they hold the Editor role. If a VM is created without specifying a service account, it uses this identity, so any code running there, including a compromised web app, can read and change most project resources. That is a serious privilege escalation risk. The better design is one dedicated service account per workload or per tier, with only the specific predefined roles it needs, attached explicitly at creation, and with access scopes set broadly while IAM does the real restriction. I strip Editor from default accounts, enforce an organization policy so new projects do not auto-grant it, disable service account key creation, prefer workload identity or impersonation over keys, and use IAM Recommender and audit logs to confirm and tune the permissions.
f: Why do access scopes still matter on VMs?
How do you migrate a running VM to a new service account?

q: How do you use IAM Recommender and Policy Intelligence to reach least privilege?
p: IAM Recommender analyses 90 days of permission usage and suggests removing or replacing roles. Policy Troubleshooter explains why access was granted or denied. Policy Analyzer shows who can access what. Together they support audits and cleanup.
tip: Apply recommendations through code review, and test in a lower environment, because rarely used permissions such as disaster recovery may not appear in the usage window.
a: Policy Intelligence is a set of tools. IAM Recommender looks at what permissions each principal has actually used over the past ninety days and recommends smaller roles or removal of unused bindings, with a count of excess permissions. Policy Troubleshooter takes a principal, resource and permission and shows exactly which bindings, conditions or deny policies produced the result, which saves a lot of time on 403 problems. Policy Analyzer answers audit questions such as who can access this bucket, or what can this service account touch, including inherited access. My process is to export recommendations regularly, review them with owners, apply changes through Terraform pull requests so they are tracked, and keep exceptions documented for rare but important access, like disaster recovery roles that are unused most of the year. I measure progress by the number of excess permissions over time.
f: What does Policy Troubleshooter show?
Why can recommendations be unsafe to auto-apply?

q: GKE Autopilot versus Standard: how do you choose?
p: Autopilot manages nodes, scaling and hardening, and bills per pod resource request. Standard gives control over node pools, machine types, DaemonSets and kernel settings, and bills per node. Choose Autopilot unless you need that control.
cmds: gcloud container clusters create-auto prod --region europe-west1
gcloud container clusters create std --region europe-west1 --num-nodes 1 --enable-autoscaling --min-nodes 1 --max-nodes 5
tip: In Autopilot, requests are what you pay for, so accurate sizing directly cuts the bill.
a: In Autopilot mode, Google manages the nodes: provisioning, upgrades, scaling, security hardening and bin-packing, and you are billed for the CPU, memory and storage that your pods request rather than for idle node capacity. It enforces good defaults such as Workload Identity, shielded nodes and restrictions on privileged containers, which lowers operational effort and risk. Standard mode gives you full control over node pools, machine types, GPUs, local SSDs, custom kernel parameters, privileged workloads and DaemonSets, but you manage capacity and pay for nodes whether they are full or not. I choose Autopilot for most general application workloads and teams with limited platform capacity. I choose Standard when workloads need special hardware or node level access, third-party agents that need privileges, or when predictable large steady usage makes committed-use node pricing cheaper. Compute classes in Autopilot cover many special cases now.
f: How are Autopilot pods billed?
What can't you do in Autopilot?

q: What are GKE release channels and maintenance windows, and how do they keep clusters current safely?
p: Rapid, Regular and Stable channels deliver Kubernetes versions at different cadences with different soak time. Cluster and node auto-upgrade follow the channel. Maintenance windows and exclusions control when upgrades happen.
cmds: gcloud container clusters update prod --region europe-west1 --release-channel regular

gcloud container clusters update prod --region europe-west1 --maintenance-window-start 2026-10-25T02:00:00Z --maintenance-window-end 2026-10-25T06:00:00Z --maintenance-window-recurrence 'FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=SU'
tip: Run dev on Rapid or Regular and production on Stable, so a version has been tested before it reaches production.
a: A release channel subscribes a cluster to a stream of Kubernetes versions that Google qualifies. Rapid gets new versions first, Regular is the default balance, and Stable receives versions that have run longer, with the most conservative cadence. Clusters on a channel are auto-upgraded, both control plane and nodes, so they never fall out of support. Maintenance windows define when automatic maintenance may start, and maintenance exclusions let me block upgrades during critical periods like a sales event, for a limited number of days, while still allowing security patches in some cases. A good strategy is to place development clusters on Rapid or Regular and production on Stable, so issues appear earlier in lower environments. I pair it with surge upgrade settings on node pools, PodDisruptionBudgets, and deprecation insights to catch removed APIs before they bite.
f: What are surge upgrades?
How do you handle a deprecated API warning?

q: How does the GKE Gateway API work compared with classic Ingress?
p: Gateway API separates roles: platform teams define a Gateway tied to a load balancer, app teams attach HTTPRoutes. It supports header routing, traffic splitting, multi-cluster gateways and policies, with Google Cloud load balancers behind it.
tip: Mention backend policies for health checks, timeouts and Cloud Armor attached through GCPBackendPolicy.
a: The classic Ingress resource is simple but limited, relying on annotations for advanced features and mixing infrastructure and application concerns in one object. The Gateway API splits this into roles. A GatewayClass identifies the implementation, for example the GKE global external managed load balancer. The platform team creates a Gateway that defines listeners, addresses and certificates. Application teams then create HTTPRoute objects in their own namespaces, which attach to the Gateway and define host and path matching, header-based routing, redirects, and weighted traffic splits for canary releases. GKE also offers multi-cluster Gateways that front services in several clusters, and policy resources for health checks, timeouts, session affinity, Cloud CDN and Cloud Armor. It gives better delegation and portability than annotations, so I use it for new designs and migrate Ingress gradually.
f: How do you do a canary with HTTPRoute?
What is a multi-cluster Gateway?

q: What are GKE node pools, node auto-provisioning and compute classes, and when do you use each?
p: Node pools are groups of identical nodes you define. Node auto-provisioning creates new pools automatically to fit pending pods within limits. Custom compute classes let workloads request ordered preferences, such as Spot first then on-demand, or specific machine families.
cmds: gcloud container node-pools create highmem --cluster prod --region europe-west1 --machine-type n2-highmem-8 --enable-autoscaling --min-nodes 0 --max-nodes 10
gcloud container clusters update prod --region europe-west1 --enable-autoprovisioning --max-cpu 500 --max-memory 2000
tip: Always set resource limits for autoprovisioning so a bad deployment cannot create unlimited nodes.
a: A node pool is a set of nodes with the same machine type, image and settings, and a cluster usually has several, for example general purpose, memory-heavy, GPU, and Spot. Each pool can use the cluster autoscaler within minimum and maximum bounds. Node auto-provisioning goes further: when pods are pending and no existing pool fits, GKE creates a new pool with a suitable machine shape, and removes it when it is empty, within the CPU, memory and GPU limits I configure. Custom compute classes let developers state in the pod spec what they prefer in priority order, like Spot on an N2D machine, then on-demand N2, and GKE will try each in turn, which balances cost and availability. I use fixed pools for stable baseline capacity and auto-provisioning or compute classes for variable and specialised workloads.
f: What limits would you set?
How do compute classes express fallback?

q: What do Config Sync and Config Connector do in a GitOps setup on GKE?
p: Config Sync continuously applies Kubernetes manifests from a Git repo to clusters and reverts drift. Config Connector exposes Google Cloud resources, such as buckets and Pub/Sub topics, as Kubernetes custom resources so they can be managed the same way.
cmds: gcloud beta container fleet config-management apply --membership=prod --config=apm.yaml
tip: Alternatives to mention: Argo CD or Flux for sync, and Terraform for cloud resources. The principle is Git as the source of truth.
a: Config Sync is part of GKE Enterprise and fleet management. It watches a Git repository, an OCI image or a Helm chart source and applies the manifests to one or many clusters, with hierarchical namespaces support, and it reverts manual changes so the cluster matches Git. This gives audited, repeatable configuration and easy rollback via git revert. Config Connector is an add-on that installs custom resource definitions for Google Cloud resources. I can declare a storage bucket, Pub/Sub topic or Cloud SQL instance as YAML, and the controller creates and reconciles it using a Google service account, so application teams manage infrastructure beside their app manifests. Alternatives are Argo CD and Flux for syncing, and Terraform or Crossplane for infrastructure. I decide by where the team already works, but the principles of Git as truth, pull-based reconciliation, and drift correction stay the same.
f: Config Connector versus Terraform?
How do you handle drift?

q: How would you design a Shared VPC for a multi-team organisation on GCP?
p: A host project owns the VPC and subnets, and service projects attach to it. Network admins control the network while project teams use subnets via the compute.networkUser role. This centralises firewalling and IP planning while keeping project-level billing and IAM.
cmds: gcloud compute shared-vpc associated-projects add svc-proj --host-project host-proj
tip: Grant networkUser at the subnet level, not the whole host project, so teams can only use their own subnets.
a: In a Shared VPC, one host project contains the VPC network, subnets, routes, firewall policies and Cloud NAT or interconnect attachments. Service projects owned by teams or environments are attached, and their resources such as VMs and GKE clusters take IP addresses from the shared subnets. A central network team manages connectivity and security, and delegates access by granting the Compute Network User role on specific subnets to the right groups. This keeps IP address planning consistent, avoids duplicate NATs and VPNs, and allows hierarchical firewall policies at the folder or organization level, while billing and quotas remain per service project. I typically create separate shared VPCs for production and non-production, plan secondary ranges for GKE pods and services, use private Google access, and monitor with VPC flow logs. Peering is used where networks must stay separate.
f: Shared VPC versus VPC peering?
How do GKE secondary ranges fit in?

q: What are Private Google Access and Private Service Connect, and how do they keep traffic off the internet?
p: Private Google Access lets VMs with only internal IPs reach Google APIs. Private Service Connect creates a private endpoint with an internal IP in your VPC for Google APIs, or for services published by others, with no peering or shared address space.
cmds: gcloud compute networks subnets update app-subnet --region europe-west1 --enable-private-ip-google-access
tip: PSC is the answer when someone asks for private access to a SaaS or a producer's service across organisations without overlapping IP problems.
a: By default a VM without an external IP cannot reach Google APIs. Enabling Private Google Access on a subnet lets such VMs reach the public API addresses of Google services using internal routing. It is a simple switch, but traffic still uses Google's public API endpoints. Private Service Connect goes further. For Google APIs, I create an endpoint with a private IP inside my VPC that forwards to an API bundle, and I can point custom DNS names to it, so on-premises networks connected via VPN or Interconnect reach APIs without any internet path. For services, PSC lets a producer publish a service attachment, and consumers create an endpoint with an IP in their VPC. The two sides do not need to share or avoid overlapping address ranges, and the connection is one-directional, which is much simpler than VPC peering for third-party services.
f: PSC versus VPC peering?
How do on-prem hosts use a PSC endpoint for APIs?

q: How do hierarchical firewall policies and VPC firewall rules work together?
p: Firewall policies can be attached to the organization, folders or networks and are evaluated top-down before VPC rules. Rules can allow, deny or delegate to the next level with goto_next. Use tags or service accounts to target workloads.
cmds: gcloud compute network-firewall-policies rules create 100 --firewall-policy corp-baseline --global-firewall-policy --action deny --direction INGRESS --src-ip-ranges 0.0.0.0/0 --layer4-configs tcp:22,tcp:3389
tip: Prefer secure tags or service account targets over network tags, since network tags can be set by anyone with VM edit rights.
a: GCP evaluates firewall policies in a fixed order: organization policy first, then folder policies, then VPC firewall rules and network-level policies, with implied rules at the end that allow all egress and deny all ingress. Inside hierarchical policies each rule can allow, deny, or use goto_next to pass the decision down to the next level. That means a central security team can enforce non-negotiable rules, such as blocking SSH and RDP from the internet or allowing health checker ranges, while delegating the rest to project owners. Rules apply to targets selected by network tags, service accounts, or secure tags. I prefer service accounts or secure tags because network tags can be changed by anyone who can edit the instance. Firewall Insights and logs show rule hit counts, shadowed rules and overly permissive rules to help with cleanup.
f: What is goto_next?
How do you find unused rules?

q: How do Cloud DNS private zones, forwarding and peering work for hybrid name resolution?
p: Private zones answer names only for attached VPCs. Forwarding zones send queries for a domain to on-premises DNS. Inbound server policies let on-premises resolvers query Cloud DNS. DNS peering shares zones between VPCs without full network peering.
tip: Hub-and-spoke DNS: host private zones in a central project and use DNS peering from spokes.
a: Cloud DNS provides several mechanisms for private name resolution. A private managed zone is visible only from the VPC networks I attach to it, which is how internal service names are resolved. A forwarding zone sends queries for a specific domain to target name servers, typically on-premises resolvers over VPN or Interconnect, and the traffic comes from a special range that the on-premises firewall must allow. For the opposite direction, an inbound server policy exposes an IP address in my VPC that on-premises resolvers can forward queries to, so they can resolve Cloud DNS private zones. DNS peering lets one VPC use the zones of another without any network peering, which supports a central DNS project with spokes. I document zone ownership, avoid overlapping namespaces, and monitor query logs when diagnosing resolution problems.
f: Why does the on-prem firewall need to allow a special range?
When would you use DNS peering?

q: GCS storage classes, Autoclass and lifecycle rules: how do you optimise storage cost?
p: Standard, Nearline, Coldline and Archive trade lower storage price for higher retrieval cost and minimum storage duration, all with the same millisecond access. Lifecycle rules transition or delete by age. Autoclass moves objects automatically based on access.
tip: Remember early deletion fees: Nearline 30 days, Coldline 90, Archive 365.
a: All storage classes offer low-latency access, but they differ in price structure. Standard is for hot data. Nearline, Coldline and Archive have lower storage prices, higher retrieval fees and minimum storage durations of thirty, ninety and three hundred sixty-five days respectively, so deleting early still incurs the charge. Lifecycle rules automate transitions and deletions, for example move to Nearline after thirty days, Coldline after ninety, and delete after a year, or remove old noncurrent versions. Autoclass is for unpredictable access patterns: it monitors object access and moves objects between classes automatically, with no retrieval fees for transitions, so I do not have to guess. I choose lifecycle rules when I know the data pattern, like logs and backups, and Autoclass for mixed data lakes. I also use regional versus multi-region buckets according to latency, availability and egress cost needs.
f: What is the early deletion fee?
When would Autoclass cost more?

q: Signed URLs and signed policy documents in Cloud Storage: how do you give temporary access safely?
p: A signed URL grants time-limited access to one object using the signer's credentials. Prefer V4 signing with a service account that has minimal access, via impersonation instead of key files. Policy documents control browser uploads.
tip: Avoid downloading service account keys just to sign. IAM Credentials signBlob works with impersonation.
a: A signed URL embeds a signature that proves a principal authorised a particular request, for a specific method, object and expiry time. Anyone with the URL can perform that action until it expires, so I keep the lifetime short and limit it to the minimum scope. The signature is created using the credentials of a service account, and that account must itself have permission on the object. To avoid creating and storing a long-lived private key, I use service account impersonation with the IAM Credentials API signBlob, granting the application the Token Creator role on a dedicated signer account. For browser uploads, a signed policy document or resumable upload URL can restrict content type and size. Alternatives for broader audiences are Cloud CDN signed URLs or signed cookies. I log access, keep buckets private with uniform bucket-level access, and rotate approaches if a URL leaks.
f: Why avoid service account key files?
Signed URL versus signed cookie?

q: Persistent Disk, Hyperdisk and Filestore: how do you choose block and file storage on GCP?
p: Persistent Disk (balanced, SSD, standard) is the default block storage. Hyperdisk lets you provision IOPS and throughput independently for demanding databases. Filestore provides managed NFS for shared access, including by GKE pods.
tip: Regional persistent disks replicate synchronously across two zones, which helps stateful workloads fail over without data loss.
a: For block storage attached to a VM or pod, Persistent Disk is the standard, with balanced as the general default, SSD for higher performance, and standard for cheap throughput. Performance scales with size, so a small disk may be slow. Hyperdisk is the newer family where I provision capacity, IOPS and throughput separately, which suits databases and other workloads that need predictable high performance without oversizing the disk, and it is required by some newer machine series. Regional disks replicate synchronously to a second zone to support failover of stateful workloads. When many nodes need the same files, such as shared content, build caches or home directories, Filestore provides managed NFS in several tiers, including enterprise with regional availability, and the Filestore CSI driver lets GKE pods use it as ReadWriteMany volumes. For object data and analytics, Cloud Storage is more suitable.
f: Regional versus zonal persistent disk?
Why does disk size affect performance?

q: How do managed instance group rolling updates, autohealing and health checks work together?
p: A MIG replaces instances gradually to a new template using maxSurge and maxUnavailable. Autohealing recreates VMs that fail an application-level health check after an initial delay. Load balancer health checks are separate and only control traffic.
cmds: gcloud compute instance-groups managed rolling-action start-update web-mig --version=template=web-v2 --max-surge=3 --max-unavailable=0 --region=europe-west1
gcloud compute instance-groups managed update web-mig --health-check=app-hc --initial-delay=300 --region=europe-west1
gcloud compute instance-groups managed describe web-mig --region=europe-west1
tip: Set the autohealing initial delay longer than your slowest boot, or healthy-but-booting VMs will be killed in a loop.
a: A managed instance group maintains identical VMs from an instance template. For updates, the rolling update policy replaces instances in batches, with maxSurge letting extra temporary instances be created and maxUnavailable limiting how many can be down, so setting maxUnavailable to zero gives zero downtime. A proactive update replaces VMs, while opportunistic updates apply only when instances are recreated for other reasons. Autohealing uses a health check to detect unresponsive applications and recreates the instance, but it only starts checking after the initial delay, which must be longer than the application's boot time. Load balancer health checks are separate: they decide whether to send traffic and do not recreate VMs, so I commonly configure both. I use regional MIGs spread across zones, and canary updates by running two template versions with a target size split for the new one.
f: What is the initial delay for?
How do you canary a template?

q: Spot VMs on GCP: how do they work and how do you use them safely?
p: Spot VMs are heavily discounted instances that Google can stop at any time with a 30-second notice and have no maximum runtime. Use them for stateless, batch or fault-tolerant work with checkpointing, and mix with on-demand capacity for baseline.
cmds: gcloud container node-pools create spot-pool --cluster prod --spot --enable-autoscaling --min-nodes 0 --max-nodes 20
tip: Poll the preempted metadata flag or handle the ACPI shutdown signal so work can checkpoint within the 30 seconds.
a: Spot VMs use spare Compute Engine capacity at a large discount, but Google may preempt them whenever it needs the resources, giving about thirty seconds of warning through the shutdown signal and a metadata flag. Unlike the older preemptible type, they have no twenty-four hour limit. Because capacity can disappear, they suit batch processing, CI workers, rendering, data pipelines and stateless web tiers behind a load balancer, provided the application checkpoints, retries or is replicated. I mix them with regular instances so the baseline is always there, spread them across zones and machine types in a managed instance group or a GKE Spot node pool, and handle the shutdown script to drain gracefully. I would not use them for databases or single points of failure. Costs and availability vary by region, so I measure the preemption rate.

q: What are OS Login and IAP TCP forwarding, and why use them instead of SSH keys and public IPs?
p: OS Login ties SSH access to IAM identities, so access and sudo are granted by roles and logged, with no key distribution. IAP TCP forwarding tunnels SSH or RDP through Google's identity-aware proxy to VMs that have no external IP.
tip: IAP needs a firewall rule allowing 35.235.240.0/20 on port 22, a detail interviewers like to hear.
a: Traditionally, SSH access is managed by adding public keys to instance or project metadata, which scatters keys, makes revocation hard and gives little audit trail. OS Login maps the Linux account to a Google identity. Access is granted with IAM roles, such as OS Login for normal users and OS Admin Login for sudo, keys are managed centrally and can be tied to two-step verification, and offboarding a person from the group removes their access everywhere. Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding addresses the network side. Instead of giving VMs public IP addresses and opening port 22 to the internet, users connect through the IAP tunnel after authentication and authorisation, so VMs can be private. A firewall rule must allow IAP's address range. Together they give private VMs, identity-based access control, and audit logs of who connected when.
f: Which IAM roles does OS Login use?
What firewall rule does IAP need?

q: How do you define SLIs and SLOs in Cloud Monitoring and alert on error budget burn?
p: Create a service, define a request-based or window-based SLI from a metric such as load balancer request count and latency, set an SLO target over a rolling or calendar window, and add burn-rate alerting policies on the error budget.
tip: Use two burn-rate windows, fast and slow, to catch sudden outages and slow leaks without constant noise.
a: In Cloud Monitoring, I model a service, for example by selecting a GKE workload, Cloud Run service or custom service, and then create an SLI. For availability, a request-based SLI is the ratio of good requests to total requests from the load balancer or application metrics. For latency, it is the proportion of requests faster than a threshold. I set an SLO target such as ninety-nine point nine percent over a rolling twenty-eight day window, which gives an error budget of the allowed bad requests. Instead of alerting on raw error rates, I create burn-rate alerts: a fast one, such as a fourteen times burn over an hour, pages immediately, and a slower one, such as a six times burn over six hours, creates a ticket. The dashboard shows remaining error budget, which informs release decisions, and I review SLOs with the product owners regularly.
f: What is a burn rate?
Request-based versus window-based SLIs?

q: How do Cloud Logging sinks, log-based metrics and exclusion filters work together?
p: Sinks route matching logs to BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub or another bucket. Log-based metrics turn log patterns into metrics for dashboards and alerts. Exclusion filters drop logs before storage to cut cost. The _Required bucket cannot be disabled.
cmds: gcloud logging metrics create http_5xx --log-filter='resource.type="k8s_container" AND jsonPayload.status>=500'
tip: Remember to grant the sink's writer identity access on the destination, a step people often forget.
a: Every log entry arrives at the Logging API and is routed through sinks. By default the Required bucket keeps audit logs and the Default bucket keeps the rest, each with its own retention. I add sinks to export filtered logs to BigQuery for analysis, Cloud Storage for cheap archive, Pub/Sub for streaming to a SIEM, or to a central logging project through an aggregated sink at the folder or organization level. The sink has a writer identity that I must grant permission on the destination. Log-based metrics count matching entries or extract values such as latency, producing counters and distributions I can chart and alert on, which is handy for application events not exposed as metrics. Exclusion filters on the Default sink drop high-volume low-value logs, for example health check requests, before they are stored. I also set retention by bucket to control cost and meet compliance.
f: Why does the sink need a writer identity?
How do you cut logging cost?

q: What is Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus, and when is it better than self-hosting Prometheus?
p: It is a managed, Prometheus-compatible backend (Monarch) that stores metrics globally, queried with PromQL. You keep exporters and PodMonitoring resources, but avoid running storage, sharding and retention yourself. Charges are per sample ingested.
cmds: gcloud container clusters update prod --region europe-west1 --enable-managed-prometheus
tip: Cost is driven by sample count, so control cardinality and scrape interval.
a: Managed Service for Prometheus provides collection and storage for Prometheus metrics without operating the Prometheus servers' scaling and long-term storage. On GKE, managed collection runs lightweight collectors as a DaemonSet, and I define scrape targets with PodMonitoring or ClusterPodMonitoring custom resources. Data is stored in Google's planet-scale Monarch backend, retained for twenty-four months, queryable across clusters and projects with PromQL from Grafana or the Cloud Monitoring UI, and can combine with Google Cloud system metrics. It is better than self-hosting when I run many clusters, need global queries, long retention, or high availability without sharding and Thanos engineering. The trade-offs are cost per ingested sample, less control over internals, and the need to manage cardinality carefully. For small, single-cluster setups, a self-managed Prometheus can still be cheaper and simpler. I always test that dashboards and alerts written in PromQL behave the same as before migrating.
f: How would you reduce sample volume?
How does it handle multi-cluster queries?

q: How do you use Secret Manager safely from applications on GCP, and handle rotation?
p: Store secrets in Secret Manager with versions and IAM at the secret level. Applications use their workload identity to access the latest or a pinned version. Rotation publishes Pub/Sub notifications that trigger a function to create a new version.
cmds: printf 's3cr3t' | gcloud secrets versions add db-password --data-file=-
tip: Pin to a version number in production and move it deliberately, rather than reading latest, to avoid surprise breakage during rotation.
a: Secret Manager stores sensitive values as versions of a secret, encrypted at rest, with fine-grained IAM and audit logging of every access. I grant the Secret Accessor role on each individual secret to the workload's own service account, rather than on the whole project. Applications read the secret at startup or on demand using client libraries, Cloud Run and Cloud Functions can inject secrets as environment variables or mounted volumes, and on GKE the Secret Manager add-on or CSI driver mounts them as files, using Workload Identity so no keys are stored. For rotation, a secret can have a rotation schedule that publishes a Pub/Sub message, which triggers a function that generates a new credential in the target system and adds a new version. Applications either reload periodically or restart. I disable or destroy old versions after a grace period, and alert on unusual access patterns.
f: Pinned version versus latest?
How does Cloud Run mount a secret?

q: What are customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) in Cloud KMS, and when are they worth the overhead?
p: By default Google encrypts data with Google-managed keys. CMEK lets you control a Cloud KMS key used to encrypt supported services, giving you rotation control, the ability to disable or destroy the key to cut access, and separate duties. It adds operational responsibility.
tip: If the key is disabled or destroyed, the data becomes unreadable. Protect key admin access and enable key destruction scheduling delays.
a: All data in Google Cloud is encrypted at rest by default with Google-managed keys. With CMEK, supported services such as Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Compute Engine disks and Cloud SQL encrypt data with a key I own in Cloud KMS, which lives in a keyring in a chosen location. The service agent receives the Encrypter Decrypter role on that key. This lets me set rotation periods, define who can administer versus use the key, audit every use in Cloud Audit Logs, and revoke access instantly by disabling the key. It is worth it for regulatory or contractual requirements, data sovereignty and separation of duties. The costs are operational: key location must match the data, a disabled key makes data unavailable, and key management adds permissions and monitoring. For stricter needs, there are Cloud HSM and External Key Manager options. I automate keys with Terraform and organization policies requiring CMEK.
f: CMEK versus CSEK?
What is Cloud EKM?

q: Which Cloud Audit Logs types exist, and which must you enable explicitly?
p: Admin Activity logs are always on and free. System Event logs are always on. Data Access logs record reads and data writes but are off by default for most services (except BigQuery) and must be enabled. Policy Denied logs record security policy denials.
tip: Data Access logs can be voluminous and costly, so enable them for sensitive services and exempt noisy service accounts.
a: Cloud Audit Logs has four categories. Admin Activity logs record API calls that modify configuration or metadata, such as creating a VM or changing IAM, they are always on, cannot be disabled and are free. System Event logs record Google-initiated changes, like live migration. Data Access logs record reads of configuration and user data, and data reads or writes, and they are disabled by default for most services because of volume and cost, so I enable them through audit configuration for sensitive services like Cloud Storage, Secret Manager and KMS, choosing admin read, data read and data write as needed. Policy Denied logs record when a request is blocked by a security policy such as VPC Service Controls. I route audit logs through an aggregated sink to a central, locked-down project, apply long retention, and build alerts on sensitive actions such as IAM changes and service account key creation.
f: Why are Data Access logs off by default?
How do you export audit logs organisation-wide?

q: What does Cloud Deploy add on top of Cloud Build for delivery to GKE and Cloud Run?
p: Cloud Build builds and tests artifacts. Cloud Deploy manages delivery pipelines across targets with promotion, approvals, canary and blue-green strategies through Skaffold, rollback, and a release audit trail.
tip: The key sentence: Build creates the artifact once, Deploy promotes the same artifact through environments.
a: Cloud Build is a general CI service that runs build steps, runs tests, builds container images and pushes them to Artifact Registry. Cloud Deploy is a managed continuous delivery service that takes those artifacts and moves them through a defined progression of targets, such as dev, staging and production. A delivery pipeline lists the targets in order, a release captures a specific set of images and manifests rendered by Skaffold, and rollouts apply them to each target. It supports approvals before production, canary and blue-green strategies for GKE and Cloud Run, automated verification steps, parallel deployments to multiple clusters, easy rollback to an earlier release, and a clear audit trail of who promoted what. This enforces the principle of building once and promoting the same immutable artifact. I use IAM so developers can create releases but only the release team can approve production.
f: Why build once and promote?
How does Cloud Deploy do a canary?

q: How do Cloud Build private pools and triggers work, and why use them for builds that touch private resources?
p: Default workers run in a Google-managed network with no access to your VPC. Private pools run in a peered network, giving builds access to private registries, databases or GKE control planes, with custom machine sizes and VPC Service Controls support.
tip: Use a dedicated user-specified service account per trigger instead of the legacy default Cloud Build account.
a: A Cloud Build trigger starts a build when something happens, such as a push to a branch, a pull request, a tag or a Pub/Sub message, and runs the steps defined in a build configuration file. By default, builds run on Google-managed workers outside my network, so they cannot reach a private GKE API endpoint, an internal artifact repository or a database. A private pool solves this by running workers in a Google-managed VPC that is peered to my VPC, so builds can reach private resources, and it supports custom machine sizes, regions and VPC Service Controls. For security I use a dedicated service account per trigger with only the roles it needs, instead of the broad default account, restrict who can edit triggers, use approval gates for sensitive triggers, and keep secrets in Secret Manager referenced by the build, not in the config.
f: Why avoid the default Cloud Build service account?
What are the limits of private pool peering?

q: How do committed use discounts work on GCP, and how do they differ from sustained use discounts?
p: Committed use discounts trade a one or three year commitment for a lower price, either resource-based (vCPU, memory) or spend-based (flexible). Sustained use discounts are automatic for some machine types and run-time, and are limited to older series. Combine with Spot for variable work.
cmds: bq query 'SELECT service.description, SUM(cost) FROM `billing.gcp_billing_export_v1_XXXX` GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC'
tip: Buy commitments for the steady baseline only, and review utilisation of the commitment monthly.
a: Committed use discounts reduce price in return for committing to a level of usage for one or three years. Resource-based commitments cover a quantity of vCPU and memory in a region, and apply automatically to matching usage, while spend-based or flexible commitments commit to a dollar amount per hour on eligible services and give more flexibility across machine families, though with a somewhat smaller discount. Sustained use discounts were an automatic discount for running certain instances for much of the month, requiring no commitment, but they apply only to some older machine series, and newer series rely on committed use instead. My approach is to analyse the stable baseline from billing export in BigQuery, commit conservatively, use Spot for interruptible capacity, shut down non-production environments out of hours, and track commitment utilisation and coverage so that money is not wasted on unused commitments.
f: Resource-based versus spend-based?
How do you size a commitment?

q: How do you set up billing export to BigQuery and labels to attribute GCP costs to teams?
p: Enable standard and detailed usage cost export to a BigQuery dataset, standardise resource labels such as team and env enforced by policy, use folders and projects as the main boundary, and build dashboards with Looker Studio on the export data.
cmds: bq query --use_legacy_sql=false 'SELECT labels.value AS team, SUM(cost) FROM `billing.gcp_billing_export_v1_X`, UNNEST(labels) AS labels WHERE labels.key="team" GROUP BY 1'
tip: Labels apply only from when they are set. They are not retroactive, so enforce them at resource creation.
a: I enable Cloud Billing export to BigQuery, the standard export for invoice-level cost and the detailed export for resource-level data, which becomes the source for all analysis. To attribute cost, the best boundary is the project, organised under folders by team or environment, which needs no tagging. Within shared projects I use labels such as team, service and environment, and enforce them with organization policy constraints, Terraform modules and checks in CI, since labels are not applied retroactively. For shared resources like GKE clusters, I enable GKE cost allocation or use namespace labels to split cost, and for shared networking I allocate proportionally. Looker Studio dashboards on the export give showback by team, and budgets with alerts to Pub/Sub or email notify owners. I also review the recommender for idle resources and rightsizing regularly.
f: Why aren't labels retroactive?
How do you attribute shared GKE costs?

q: BigQuery on-demand versus capacity (slot) pricing: how do you choose and control query cost?
p: On-demand charges per TB scanned and shares a pool of slots. Capacity pricing buys dedicated slots with editions and autoscaling, giving predictable cost for heavy workloads. Control cost with partitioning, clustering, selecting only needed columns, and quotas.
tip: Always partition large tables on a date column and require a partition filter to prevent accidental full scans.
a: With on-demand pricing, I pay for the bytes each query processes, so cost depends on how well queries limit data scanned, and I get access to a shared pool of slots. With capacity pricing, I purchase slots in an edition, with autoscaling and optional commitments, and pay for slot-hours regardless of how much data is scanned, which suits steady heavy analytics and gives predictable cost and workload isolation through reservations and assignments. To control costs on either model, I partition tables by date and cluster by frequently filtered columns, select only needed columns rather than select star, require partition filters, use dry runs to estimate bytes, set maximum bytes billed on queries, apply project and user-level quotas, use materialised views or summary tables for repeated dashboards, and monitor the INFORMATION_SCHEMA jobs views to find expensive queries and users.
f: What does clustering do?
How does a dry run help?

q: GKE pods are Pending with 'Insufficient' errors or IP allocation failures. How do you diagnose it?
p: Distinguish resource shortage from IP exhaustion. Check pod events, node allocatable versus requests, autoscaler status, and the pod secondary range utilisation. VPC-native clusters allocate a /24 slice of the pod range per node, which can run out.
cmds: gcloud container clusters describe prod --region europe-west1 --format='yaml(ipAllocationPolicy,defaultMaxPodsConstraint)'
tip: Lower max pods per node or add a discontiguous pod range to extend a cluster that ran out of pod IPs.
a: The pod events say whether the scheduler failed because no node has enough CPU or memory, or because of taints and affinity, or whether the node cannot assign an IP. For resource shortage, I check requested versus allocatable resources, whether the cluster autoscaler is enabled, and whether it is blocked by quota or maximum node limits. For IP problems, in a VPC-native cluster the pod secondary range is carved into per-node blocks, by default a /24 per node for one hundred ten pods, so a small pod range limits the number of nodes, and the primary subnet range limits the node count as well. Fixes include adding discontiguous multi-pod CIDR ranges, reducing max pods per node so smaller blocks are used, enlarging subnets in a new node pool, or creating a new cluster with a larger plan. I prevent it by calculating the IP budget during design and monitoring utilisation.
f: What is a discontiguous multi-pod CIDR?
How does max pods per node affect IP use?

q: A GKE Ingress or Gateway returns 502 errors and the backend shows as unhealthy. What do you check?
p: The Google load balancer health check must succeed against the pod. Check that firewall rules allow Google health check ranges, the readiness probe and health check path match, container-native NEGs are in use, and the app listens on the target port.
tip: The load balancer health check is derived from the readiness probe by default, but only if the path and port are compatible.
a: I check the backend health first, which shows which endpoints are unhealthy. The Google Cloud load balancer probes from specific ranges, one thirty dot two eleven dot zero dot zero slash twenty-two and thirty-five dot one ninety-one dot zero dot zero slash sixteen, so a firewall rule must allow them to reach the pods or nodes on the serving port. Next the health check configuration: by default GKE infers it from the pod's readiness probe, but if the path returns a redirect or non-200 status, or the probe is on a different port, the check fails. A BackendConfig or HealthCheckPolicy lets me set the path, port and thresholds explicitly. I confirm the app listens on the right port and interface, that container-native load balancing with NEGs is used so traffic goes directly to pods, and that pods are ready. For intermittent 502s, I examine connection draining, keep-alive timeouts, and the backend timeout setting.
f: Why are NEGs better than instance groups?
Which ranges do Google health checks use?

q: A GKE node auto-upgrade broke workloads. How do you reduce the blast radius next time?
p: Identify what changed: a Kubernetes version removing an API or changing behaviour, node image changes, or workloads that cannot tolerate disruption. Use release channels with soak, maintenance windows and exclusions, surge settings, PDBs, and test in staging.
cmds: gcloud container node-pools update pool1 --cluster prod --region europe-west1 --max-surge-upgrade 2 --max-unavailable-upgrade 0
tip: For a risky window, use a maintenance exclusion, and for a rollback create a new pool on the old version if the old minor is still supported.
a: First I identify exactly what changed by reading the upgrade operation, release notes for the new version, and cluster events. Common causes are a removed or changed API that a controller still used, a different default such as a container runtime or kernel behaviour, a node image update that changed a driver, or workloads with single replicas and no disruption budget being evicted at the same time. To recover, I fix the workload or roll traffic to a new node pool built from the previous version, since control planes cannot be downgraded. To reduce the blast radius in future, I run staging clusters on a faster channel so I see the version first, use maintenance windows and exclusions, set surge upgrade with zero max unavailable, ensure PodDisruptionBudgets and at least two replicas, check deprecation insights before each upgrade, and use blue-green node pool upgrades for critical clusters.
f: Can you downgrade a GKE control plane?
What is blue-green node pool upgrade?

q: A pod using Workload Identity cannot access Google APIs and gets 403 or metadata server errors. How do you fix it?
p: Check that Workload Identity is enabled on the cluster and node pool, the Kubernetes service account is annotated with the Google service account, the IAM binding grants roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser to the right namespace and name, and the GSA has the needed permissions.
cmds: kubectl get sa app -n prod -o yaml | grep iam.gke.io
tip: The member format is serviceAccount:PROJECT.svc.id.goog[NAMESPACE/KSA]. A typo there is the most common cause.
a: I run a curl against the metadata server from inside the pod to see which identity it receives. If it shows the node's default service account or fails, Workload Identity is not active for that pod. I check that the cluster has a workload pool configured and the node pool uses the GKE metadata server, since older pools may not. Then I confirm the Kubernetes service account has the iam.gke.io slash gcp-service-account annotation pointing to the right Google service account. On the Google side, that account must grant the Workload Identity User role to the member string with the project's workload pool, namespace and service account name, exactly matched. Finally, the Google service account itself needs the API permissions, such as Storage Object Viewer. Newer clusters can bind IAM directly to the Kubernetes service account principal without annotation, which simplifies the setup.
f: What is the principal format for direct binding?
Why does the metadata server matter?

q: The GKE cluster autoscaler is not adding nodes though pods are Pending. What are the usual causes on GCP?
p: Quota limits (CPUs, IPs, disks), max node count reached, no node pool that fits the pod's requests, selectors or zone constraints, a PVC bound to a zone with no capacity, or stockouts of a machine type in a zone.
cmds: gcloud container clusters describe prod --region europe-west1 --format='yaml(autoscaling,nodePools[].autoscaling)'
gcloud compute regions describe europe-west1 --format='yaml(quotas)' | grep -B1 -A1 'CPUS\|IN_USE_ADDRESSES'
tip: Use multiple zones and machine types, or node auto-provisioning, to reduce zonal stockout failures.
a: The pod's NotTriggerScaleUp event explains why existing pools were rejected. If the pod requests more resources than the largest machine in any pool, no scale-up can help, so I fix the request or add a larger pool. If a node selector, taint or affinity matches no pool, autoscaling cannot satisfy it. If the pool is at its maximum size, I raise it. Then I check Google Cloud causes: project quotas for CPUs, in-use IP addresses or persistent disk capacity, and zonal resource exhaustion where the machine type is temporarily unavailable, which the autoscaler logs as a scale-up failure. A PersistentVolume bound to a specific zone limits where the pod can go. Remedies are raising quotas, spreading pools across zones and using several machine families, enabling node auto-provisioning, and adding alerts on pending pods and autoscaler errors.
f: How does a zonal stockout appear?
What does NotTriggerScaleUp mean?

q: Cloud Run cannot connect to Cloud SQL or a private service in your VPC. How do you set up connectivity?
p: Cloud Run is serverless and outside your VPC by default. Use the Cloud SQL connection (unix socket via the Auth proxy built-in) for Cloud SQL, and Direct VPC egress or a Serverless VPC Access connector for private IPs, with correct firewall rules and egress setting.
cmds: gcloud run services describe api --region europe-west1 --format='yaml(spec.template.metadata.annotations)'
tip: The Cloud Run service account needs the Cloud SQL Client role, a frequent missing piece.
a: For Cloud SQL, I can attach the instance to the Cloud Run service, which exposes a Unix socket at slash cloudsql, and the application connects through it using the connection name. The service account needs the Cloud SQL Client role, and for private IP instances the service also needs VPC connectivity. For other private resources, such as internal load balancers, Memorystore or VMs, I configure Direct VPC egress, which assigns the service addresses from a subnet, or a Serverless VPC Access connector. I choose whether all egress or only private ranges go through the VPC, because sending all traffic through requires Cloud NAT for internet access. Firewall rules must allow traffic from the subnet or connector range to the destination. If connections fail, I check the service account roles, the egress setting, DNS resolution for private names, connection limits, and that the instance has the right IP configuration.
f: Direct VPC egress versus connector?
Why might all-traffic egress break internet calls?

q: A Pub/Sub subscription backlog keeps growing. How do you investigate and fix it?
p: Compare publish rate to ack rate, check oldest unacked message age, subscriber errors and ack deadline expirations, then scale subscribers, tune flow control, fix poison messages with dead-letter topics, and look at downstream dependencies.
tip: Alert on oldest_unacked_message_age, not just message count, since age directly maps to user-visible delay.
a: I start with the metrics: undelivered message count, oldest unacked message age, delivery attempts, and ack and nack rates compared with the publish rate. If subscribers are healthy but too few, I scale them out, or switch to streaming pull with larger flow control settings. If messages are repeatedly redelivered, the ack deadline may be shorter than the processing time, so I extend it or use lease extensions in the client library. A poison message that always fails can block ordered delivery or consume retries, so I add a dead-letter topic with a maximum delivery attempt count and investigate the dead letters. Downstream bottlenecks, such as a slow database, are also a common cause, so I check dependency latency and apply backpressure. I set alerts on message age and dead-letter volume, and make handlers idempotent since delivery is at least once.
f: Why is delivery at least once?
How does ordering affect the backlog?

q: Cloud NAT drops connections with 'OUT_OF_RESOURCES' or allocation failures under load. What is the cause and fix?
p: Each NAT IP provides about 64,512 ports, divided among VMs. When a VM exhausts its allocated ports to the same destination, new connections fail. Raise minimum ports per VM, add NAT IPs, enable dynamic port allocation, and reuse connections.
cmds: gcloud compute routers nats describe nat1 --router=rtr1 --region=europe-west1
gcloud compute routers nats update nat1 --router=rtr1 --region=europe-west1 --enable-dynamic-port-allocation --min-ports-per-vm=128 --max-ports-per-vm=4096
tip: Connection pooling and keep-alive in the application is the cheapest fix, since it removes the need for so many ports.
a: Cloud NAT translates private addresses to external IPs by allocating source ports. A NAT IP address has around sixty-four thousand ports, and with a configured minimum ports per VM, each VM gets a block. Many simultaneous connections to the same destination IP, port and protocol can consume all of a VM's ports, and then new connections are dropped, which shows in NAT logs as dropped allocation status and in the dropped-sent-packets metric. Solutions are to enable dynamic port allocation so busy VMs can get more ports, raise minimum ports per VM, add more NAT IP addresses or use automatic allocation, shorten timeouts for idle connections, and most importantly use connection pooling and keep-alive in clients so they don't open a new connection per request. For GKE, I also consider whether many pods behind one node share the port range. Monitoring the allocation metrics provides early warning.
f: What is dynamic port allocation?
Why do many connections to one destination cause the problem?

q: A request is denied by VPC Service Controls and the team cannot reach a service from their CI system. How do you investigate and fix it safely?
p: Look up the violation in audit logs (Policy Denied) for the unique ID, which shows the source identity, network, service and which rule it breached. Fix with an ingress or egress rule scoped to the specific identity, project and method, or an access level, rather than loosening the perimeter.
cmds: gcloud access-context-manager perimeters dry-run update prod-perimeter --policy=POLICY_ID --add-ingress-policies=ingress.yaml
tip: Test changes in dry-run mode first, which logs would-be violations without enforcing.
a: VPC Service Controls draw a perimeter around projects and services to block data exfiltration, so a request from outside, such as a CI runner in another project or from an unknown network, gets a 403 with a unique violation identifier. I search the audit logs for that ID, which names the caller identity, the source project or IP, the target service and method, and the reason, for example not in the same perimeter or no matching access level. Then I choose the narrowest fix: add the CI project into the perimeter, create an ingress rule allowing that service account to call specific methods on specific services, or an egress rule for legitimate outbound access, or an access level based on IP or device. I test the change in dry-run mode, review the logs, then enforce. I avoid disabling the perimeter or adding broad allowances, and I document each exception with an owner and expiry.
f: Ingress versus egress rules?
What is dry-run mode?

q: A deployment fails with 'Permission denied' even though the engineer has Owner. Which other layers could be blocking it?
p: Owner can still be blocked by organisation policies, IAM deny policies, VPC Service Controls, missing API enablement, billing issues, or quotas. Use Policy Troubleshooter and the error's details to find which layer denied the call.
tip: Read the full error. Organisation policy errors name the constraint, like constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess.
a: Having a powerful role is only one input. The error text tells me which layer refused. A message naming a constraint, such as restricting external IPs or allowed regions, comes from an organization policy, which applies regardless of IAM role. A deny policy at a higher level blocks specific permissions even for owners. VPC Service Controls can reject calls from outside the perimeter. An API that is not enabled in the project returns a different error, as do billing being disabled or quota exhaustion. Policy Troubleshooter is the tool to confirm the IAM side, as it shows allow, deny and condition evaluation. If it is an org policy, I either change the design, for example use a private IP and NAT, or request an exception with the right approvers, applying it at the lowest sensible scope. I avoid granting more roles to work around a guardrail.
f: What is the difference between org policy and IAM?
How do you request an org policy exception?

q: Terraform on GCP fails with 'API has not been used in project' or 'service account does not have permission'. How do you make it reliable?
p: Enable required APIs explicitly with google_project_service, wait for propagation using dependencies, grant the Terraform service account the needed roles, and check the right quota project and impersonation settings. Split bootstrap from application stacks.
cmds: gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com container.googleapis.com --project my-proj
tip: Use depends_on or the service resource output as a dependency so resources do not race the API enablement.
a: The first error means the API is disabled in the project, or was just enabled and has not propagated. I manage API enablement in Terraform with google_project_service resources, and make dependent resources depend on them, sometimes with a short delay or retry. For permission errors, I check which identity Terraform is actually using: a user's application default credentials, a service account key, or impersonation of a deployer service account. That identity needs the right roles in the target project, plus Service Usage Consumer, and the quota project setting must point to a project where the API is enabled. For reliability, I use a dedicated deployer service account through impersonation or workload identity federation in CI, split a bootstrap stack that creates projects, APIs and service accounts from the application stacks, store state in a versioned bucket with locking, and run plan checks before apply.
f: Why impersonate a service account in Terraform?
What is the quota project?

q: GKE cannot pull images from Artifact Registry and shows 403 or ImagePullBackOff. What do you check?
p: The node service account needs Artifact Registry Reader on the repository, the repository must be in a reachable location, private clusters need Private Google Access, and image paths must be exact. Check cross-project permissions and VPC Service Controls.
cmds: gcloud artifacts docker images list europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/proj/repo
tip: With custom node service accounts, remember to grant them the Reader role. Only the default account may have had it implicitly.
a: The pod events show whether it is an authorization error, a not found error, or a network timeout. For a 403, the identity pulling images is the node's service account, so it needs the Artifact Registry Reader role on the repository or project, which is easy to forget when using a custom node service account instead of the default one. For cross-project pulls, the grant has to be on the project that owns the repository. For not found, I verify the full path, which includes location, project, repository, image name and tag, and that the tag exists. For timeouts in a private cluster, nodes without external IPs need Private Google Access or Cloud NAT to reach the registry endpoint. VPC Service Controls may also block the pull if the registry is in a different perimeter. I fix the specific cause and test with a manual pull from a debug pod or with crictl on a node.
f: Which identity pulls images on GKE?
How do you pull across projects?

q: A large GCP network egress charge appeared. How do you find the traffic and reduce it?
p: Use billing export by SKU to see whether it is internet egress, inter-region, inter-zone or CDN. Then VPC Flow Logs and Network Intelligence to find sources and destinations. Reduce with Cloud CDN, regional co-location, compression, caching, and private paths.
cmds: bq query --use_legacy_sql=false 'SELECT sku.description, SUM(cost) c FROM `billing.gcp_billing_export_v1_X` WHERE service.description="Compute Engine" AND sku.description LIKE "%Egress%" GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY c DESC'
gcloud compute networks subnets update app --region=europe-west1 --enable-flow-logs --logging-aggregation-interval=interval-5-min
tip: Cross-zone and cross-region traffic inside the same app is a quiet cost, so check topology before blaming the internet.
a: I begin by identifying which kind of egress it is, using the billing export grouped by SKU. Internet egress, inter-region transfer and inter-zone traffic have different prices and different fixes. Then I enable VPC Flow Logs, with sampling, on the relevant subnets and query them in BigQuery to find top talkers by source, destination and bytes, and use Network Intelligence Center to view the topology. Typical causes are large downloads served straight from instances or buckets without caching, chatty services spread across regions or zones, backups or replication to another region, and analytics exports. Remedies include putting Cloud CDN or an edge cache in front of static content, serving from the same region as the consumers, compressing payloads, using zonal affinity so traffic stays within a zone, moving heavy data jobs next to the data, and choosing the correct network service tier. I add a budget alert for network SKUs.
f: Premium versus Standard network tier?
How do you keep traffic within a zone?

q: Cloud Logging costs have exploded. How do you identify the source and reduce them without losing important logs?
p: Use Logs Explorer and the log volume metrics to see bytes ingested by resource and log name. Typical culprits are debug logging, load balancer or VPC flow logs, and chatty GKE containers. Add exclusion filters, sampling, routing to cheaper storage, and retention changes.
tip: The logging/billing/bytes_ingested metric by resource_type quickly shows who generates the volume.
a: I look at the ingestion volume metrics, which break bytes down by resource type and log name, to find the main producers. Common ones are a service accidentally left at debug level, GKE container stdout from a crash-looping pod, Data Access audit logs on busy services, VPC flow logs at a high sampling rate, and load balancer logs for every request. For each source, I decide the right action: reduce the log level in the application, fix the loop, lower the flow log sampling, or add exclusion filters on the Default sink to drop low-value entries such as health check requests, with sampling when I still want a fraction. Some logs are still required for audit or security, so I route those through a sink to a cheaper destination like Cloud Storage for retention, set shorter retention on the Default bucket, and create budget alerts on Logging spend. I review volume monthly.
f: Exclusion filter versus sampling?
What must never be excluded?

q: A log sink to BigQuery is not receiving data. What do you check?
p: Verify the sink's filter matches entries, the sink's writer identity has BigQuery Data Editor on the dataset, the destination dataset exists in an allowed location, the sink is not disabled or excluded upstream, and check for sink errors in the logs.
tip: The writer identity is created per sink. Copy it from the describe output and grant it on the destination, every time.
a: First I describe the sink to confirm it is enabled and see its filter and writer identity. Then I test the filter in Logs Explorer to be sure matching entries exist for the time period. The most common problem is permissions: the writer identity, a service account unique to the sink, must have the BigQuery Data Editor role on the destination dataset, and if the sink is at the organization level with include children, I need to check that the identity is unique per sink. The destination dataset must exist, and be in a location that the sink supports, and for partitioned tables the settings must match. Exclusion filters on the sink or on the log bucket can drop entries, and organization policies such as restricting resource locations can block creation of tables. Sink errors are written to the logs of the project, so I search there. After fixing, new entries should appear within minutes.
f: Why is the writer identity unique?
Can a sink export old logs?

q: A managed instance group keeps recreating instances in an autohealing loop. How do you stop it and find the cause?
p: Instances are failing the autohealing health check, often because the initial delay is too short, the check path or port is wrong, a firewall blocks health check ranges, or the app crashes under load. Disable autohealing temporarily, inspect an instance, then fix.
cmds: gcloud compute instance-groups managed list-errors web-mig --region=europe-west1
gcloud compute instance-groups managed update web-mig --clear-autohealing --region=europe-west1
tip: The serial port output shows startup script failures, which are a frequent root cause for new instances never becoming healthy.
a: A loop means each new VM fails its health check and is replaced before it can stabilise. I list the group's errors and recent operations to confirm autohealing is the actor. To stop the churn while I investigate, I temporarily remove autohealing or lengthen the initial delay. Then I take a failing instance, check the serial console output and startup script logs, and curl the health check path from the instance. Typical causes: the initial delay is shorter than boot plus warm-up time, the health check uses the wrong port or path or expects a status the app does not return, the firewall does not allow the Google health check ranges, a startup script fails because of a missing secret or unreachable dependency, or the app is overloaded and fails checks under load. After fixing it, I re-enable autohealing with a realistic delay and thresholds, and bake images to shorten boot time.
f: Which ranges do health checks come from?
Why bake images instead of using startup scripts?

q: A Cloud VPN tunnel is established but BGP is down or routes are missing on-premises. How do you troubleshoot?
p: Check tunnel status and IKE logs, then BGP peer settings: ASNs, link-local IPs, MD5 if used, and Cloud Router advertised routes. Verify firewalls on both sides and that overlapping ranges are not present. Use route and learned-route views.
tip: Tunnel up and BGP down usually points to an ASN or link-local address mismatch, or a firewall dropping TCP 179.
a: I separate the layers. First, tunnel status: if it is not established, the IKE settings, shared secret, peer IP, or on-premises firewall rules for UDP 500 and 4500 are wrong, and the VPN logs show negotiation failures. If the tunnel is established but BGP is down, I compare both sides on the ASNs, the link-local tunnel inside addresses, any authentication, and verify that TCP port 179 is allowed through the tunnel. Once BGP is up but routes are missing, I look at what Cloud Router advertises: by default it advertises subnets according to the dynamic routing mode, so I may need custom advertised ranges, and at the learned routes from the peer. Overlapping address ranges, route priority conflicts, and regional versus global routing mode can cause surprises. For production I use HA VPN with two tunnels and BGP and test failover.

q: A Compute Engine persistent disk is almost full. How do you grow it online and avoid a repeat?
p: Resize the disk with gcloud, which works while attached, then grow the partition and filesystem in the guest. Take a snapshot first. Find the cause of growth and add monitoring with the Ops Agent for disk usage alerts.
tip: Disks can only grow, never shrink, so go up in measured steps.
a: I start by snapshotting the disk, since resizing is generally safe but a restore point costs little. Then I increase the size with the resize command, which can be done while the disk is attached and the VM is running. Inside the guest, I extend the partition with growpart if the filesystem sits on a partition, and then grow the filesystem with resize2fs for ext4 or xfs_growfs for XFS. The size cannot be reduced later, so I increase by a sensible amount. For the root cause, I check what consumed the space, using du, looking at logs, temp files, database data or deleted-but-open files, and fix log rotation or add retention. Disk utilisation is not visible without an agent, so I install the Ops Agent, create an alert at eighty percent, and consider moving growing data to a separate data disk with automation to expand it.

How does the Ops Agent expose disk usage?

q: A Security Command Center finding reports a publicly accessible Cloud Storage bucket. How do you respond?
p: Confirm whether the exposure is intended, then remove public access, enable public access prevention and uniform bucket-level access, check access logs for what was read, and fix the pipeline or policy that allowed it. Use org policy to stop recurrence.
cmds: gcloud storage buckets get-iam-policy gs://my-bucket --format=json | grep -E 'allUsers|allAuthenticatedUsers'
tip: Check Data Access audit logs, if enabled, to see whether anyone actually read objects while it was public.
a: First I validate the finding: look at the bucket policy for allUsers or allAuthenticatedUsers, and find out with the owner whether the exposure was intended, such as a static website, or an accident. If it is not intended, I immediately remove the public bindings and turn on public access prevention, plus uniform bucket-level access so ACLs on individual objects cannot re-expose data. Then I assess impact: review Data Access and request logs, if they were enabled, to see which objects were fetched and from where, classify what data was inside with Sensitive Data Protection, and involve incident response or privacy teams if needed. To prevent a recurrence, I enforce the organization policy for public access prevention, scan Terraform in CI for public bindings, set Security Command Center notifications to a chat or ticketing channel, and educate teams about safer sharing options such as signed URLs or a CDN.
f: What is Sensitive Data Protection?
Why prefer uniform bucket-level access?

q: Spot VM or Spot GKE node preemptions are causing batch jobs to fail. How do you make them resilient?
p: Make work restartable: checkpoint progress, make tasks idempotent, use a queue so unfinished tasks return, handle the shutdown signal to save state, diversify zones and machine types, and keep a small on-demand pool to guarantee completion.
tip: Measure preemption frequency. If a job is shorter than the typical time between preemptions, retries are cheap.
a: With Spot capacity, interruptions are normal, so the design must expect them. I split big jobs into smaller idempotent tasks put on a queue such as Pub/Sub or Cloud Tasks, so if a worker disappears, its unacknowledged task is delivered again. For long computations, I checkpoint intermediate state to Cloud Storage regularly and resume from the latest checkpoint. A shutdown script or signal handler uses the thirty-second warning to flush state and release locks. To reduce correlated loss, I spread workers across several zones and machine types in a regional managed instance group or multiple GKE node pools. I keep a small on-demand pool or fallback so deadlines are met even when Spot capacity is scarce, and set sensible retry limits and backoff. For Kubernetes, Job backoffLimit and Indexed Jobs help. I track preemption rates and the cost-per-completed-job to verify the savings.
